name: Tools
simple: Tools are the model's hands (act) and eyes (read). A brain with no tools can only talk — and will hallucinate, because it can't perceive or reach the real world.
how: A skill is the recipe, a tool is the callable — the skill REFERENCES the tool, never the reverse.
The harness loads the matched skill into context BEFORE the model acts, so it picks the right tool and grounds its reply in the real result instead of guessing.
MCP (strict schema) for the customer agent; Code Mode (23 tools → 2) for the admin agent — trust-tiered, ~60% fewer input tokens.
killer: Tools give the model hands. Harness engineering decides what those hands are allowed to touch.

name: Context
q: What does it see this step?
simple: Context is everything in front of the model for one call — system prompt, skills, history, tool results. The model knows nothing else.
how: What separates one agent from another is ~90% context (prompt + tools + MCP + db-scope + skills); the only non-context part is the model itself.
3-tier lazy loading: system prompt → keyword-matched skill → api_search fallback, scoped per-tenant from tenant_files by account_id.
Agent = Model + Context, so multiple agents are just multiple context bundles on the same brain.
killer: Context is the model's entire reality for that step — control it and you control behavior.

name: Control Flow
simple: The traffic controller around the brain — when to run the model, call a tool, retry, or stop. Cheap deterministic checks first, the expensive model last.
how: Six cheap gates run BEFORE the LLM: self-message, valid payload, dedup, lock, human-handling, credits.
The agent loop is bounded — it stops on no-tool-call, a 20-turn cap, a 2-min timeout, or an isolation abort.
Fire-and-forget 202 — the webhook returns instantly while the agent works in the background.
killer: Most of my control flow runs before the model: cheap deterministic checks first, the expensive model last.

name: Guardrails
q: What is it forbidden to do?
simple: The locks the AI physically cannot break — like a smart new staff member you don't fully trust yet. They live in CODE (100% deterministic), not the prompt (~98%) — you can't protect money or records with 'probably'.
how: Tenant isolation: the server OVERRIDES account_id — the AI can't even choose whose data it sees.
Refunds are hard-blocked (LOCKED_REVIEW_ACTIONS) — the AI can ask, but a human must approve.
Internal notes and tags are stripped before the customer ever sees the message.
killer: The model can't pick the tenant — the server sets account_id. The LLM is an input, not an authority.

name: Memory
simple: Without memory the agent is a goldfish. Memory lets it remember the customer across a conversation and across days.
how: Tiered storage: SQLite+vec (agent memory), Postgres (company truth), Qdrant (scale).
A dedicated memory agent retrieves it; the LLM only orchestrates while a local embedder + reranker do the heavy lifting.
Recall and voting cost ZERO LLM tokens; a verifier checks 9 failure modes before the answer ships.
killer: Heavy lifting is done by local embedder + reranker — the LLM only orchestrates.

name: Reliability
simple: When something breaks, the AI doesn't die — it has a backup plan. Four kinds: backup, retry, timeout, degrade.
how: 7 failure points, each with a matched plan: per-turn model fallback, 2-min timeout, 20-turn loop cap, MCP health check, session sanitizer, stale-session retry, 503 load-shed.
Fallback is per-turn, not per-request — a backup model retries just the failed turn.
The skill is matching the plan to the failure — not retries everywhere (retrying a refund could double-charge).
killer: I designed for failure, not just the happy path.

name: Observability
q: How do I see what it did?
simple: The window into an autonomous agent — so when something goes wrong you can see why, not guess. Without it, a 'wrong price' complaint has no record.
how: OpenTelemetry/OTLP → Tempo (traces) + Prometheus (metrics) → Grafana (dashboards).
Per-request metrics (path, status, latency) land in TimescaleDB, flushed every 60s.
Every metric carries account_id → per-tenant visibility, not just system averages.
killer: Not just 'the system is up' — I can prove THIS customer is being served well.

name: Runtime Cost
q: How much per reply — and cap it?
simple: The petrol, not the car. Build cost is paid once; runtime cost is paid per reply, forever.
how: Two sides: tokens I pay the LLM + credits the customer pays me — the credit system is the bridge that keeps them aligned.
Biggest lever = input tokens (re-sent every turn) → cut via Code Mode + lazy loading + history limit + zero-LLM recall.
Credit gate runs BEFORE the LLM (race-safe SELECT FOR UPDATE), with a deliberate fail-open so a billing outage never blocks a customer.
killer: My biggest cost is input tokens, paid every turn — so I optimized what's IN context, not what comes out.

name: Human-in-the-Loop
simple: A designed checkpoint, not a failure. Some decisions are too risky to let the AI make alone.
how: Risky actions (refunds, returns) are blocked and queued for human approval.
Per-action risk tiers — auto / review / block — let each tenant set its own appetite.
Dangerous actions are pinned to 'review' and cannot be downgraded — a safety floor.
killer: I don't hardcode what needs a human — it's a per-tenant policy with a non-downgradable floor.

name: Evaluation
q: How do I know it's correct?
simple: Testing if the AI's answers are correct, like giving a student an exam. My honest weak spot — and a roadmap.
how: Offline (staging) via promptfoo: golden tests, regression, red-team, model comparison — runs in CI.
Online (production): live reply sampling + CSAT + an inline verifier — the gap I still need to build.
AI is probabilistic, so you can't exact-match — you grade fuzzily (keyword / LLM-judge / human).
killer: I can prove the agent is safe and cheap; proving it's measurably accurate over time is my next build.
